gap: No result ChatGPT got states that The Technology Man measured the BLUETTI FridgePower's idle draw at 12.1 W, three times the 4 W BLUETTI claims. Over a day that is about 290 Wh, which cuts the reviewer's own 4.1-day estimate (1,749 Wh usable for a fridge using 427 Wh a day) to about 2.4 days. So anyone who wants two or more days should buy the FridgePower + BlueCell 200 bundle, not the base unit.
standout_why: I compared five pages. itechguides.com, which ChatGPT cited, prints only the makers' idle claims (BLUETTI 'as low as 4 W', Anker '6W idle'), with no measured figure and no runtime cost. basc.pnnl.gov, also cited, gives daily-energy sizing (EnergyGuide kWh ÷ 365, 630 kWh/yr ≈ 1.7 kWh/day) but says nothing about the inverter's own draw. powerstations.reviews lists the FridgePower at $899–949 with no idle-draw or car-charging figures. The two pages that came back from searches I ran but that ChatGPT did not get (readyhomesystems.com on ECO auto-off; aphnetworks.com, which only appeared as a search title and I did not open) also lack a measured idle figure for this unit. No rival page gives a measured idle draw for any unit, or the 108 W ceiling for charging from a car's 12 V socket. Rivals do already cover the energy meter and the thermometer.
kit_items: Power station (UPS, sits at the fridge): BLUETTI FridgePower, 2,016 Wh LiFePO4, 1,800 W continuous / 3,600 W surge. BLUETTI claims under 10 ms switchover and The Technology Man measured 6.2 ms, so the fridge never notices an outage. Brackets in the box let it sit beside the fridge, on top or on a wall.

Expansion battery: BLUETTI BlueCell 200 (in the FridgePower + BC200 bundle). Once the measured 12.1 W idle draw is counted, the base unit covers about 2.4 days of a 427 Wh/day fridge. A 630 kWh/yr fridge, the basc.pnnl.gov example, uses about 1.7 kWh/day, which with 290 Wh/day of idle draw is about 2 kWh/day, so the base unit covers it for under a day. Two or more days need the expansion.

Recharge path for long outages: BLUETTI Charger 2 (FridgePower + Charger 2 + DC Hub bundle). The Technology Man measured only 108 W from a car's 12 V socket into the FridgePower's XT60 input. That is roughly 3.6 hours of fridge-plus-idle load per hour of charging, so the 12 V socket alone is too slow for a multi-day outage.
Plug-in energy meter (any brand, not sold by BLUETTI): basc.pnnl.gov says to meter an existing fridge for several days. That reading sets whether you need the BC200.
Fridge thermometer (any brand): the FDA setpoint is 40 °F or lower, per basc.pnnl.gov.

findings.note: Gidon measured it over 20 hours with AC on and no load. 12.1 W × 24 h = 290 Wh/day. The reviewer appears to be Australian, so this may be the 230 V unit; the US 120 V idle figure could differ.

findings.label: Runtime with idle draw counted (reviewer's fridge)
findings.value: ≈2.4 days, versus the 'just over four days' the reviewer calculated
findings.note: The reviewer's fridge averaged 427 Wh/day over 30 days. 427 + 290 (idle) = 717 Wh/day; 1,749 ÷ 717 = 2.44 days. The reviewer's 4.1 days is 1,749 ÷ 427, which leaves idle out. Assumes the no-load idle draw carries over while the fridge runs.

findings.label: Measured car charging from a 12 V socket
findings.value: 108 W at about 13.5 V; just over 220 W from 24 V
findings.note: Through the single XT60 input (12–60 V, up to 20 A). 108 W ÷ ~30 W average load (717 Wh ÷ 24 h) ≈ 3.6 h of runtime per hour of charging. Two 200 W panels gave about 300 W on a sunny, partly cloudy day.
